why: A refresh that faults must end the inner sequence, not the outer subscription. Rethrowing kills the deferred-refresh stream permanently, so the list silently stops updating.
The whole point of the prefix clause. A revert costs the index and re-sorts the library, but produces a byte-identical query plan - only a structural assertion catches it.

why: The clause prefix and the index expression must agree. Changing one and not the other silently drops back to a full sort.

substr() returns a BINARY result and does not inherit the column collation, so both terms must name NOCASE explicitly. If the tie-break drifts back to BINARY the two halves of the ORDER BY disagree about what 'less than' means and the result is neither order.
find: substr(c.content, 1, 64) COLLATE NOCASE ASC, c.content COLLATE NOCASE ASC
replace: substr(c.content, 1, 64) COLLATE NOCASE ASC, c.content COLLATE BINARY ASC

why: Every sort needs its own pinned-prefixed index. Without one, the sort falls back to a temp B-tree over the whole library (252ms at 20k clips).
Same, for the expression index. Partial index coverage measured worse than none at all.
Disabling a sensitivity rule stops having any effect. Found by audit: this survived all 278 non-headless tests before SensitivityServiceTests existed.
Scan runs on the capture path against user-authored regexes. Unbounded backtracking hangs clipboard capture: "(a+)+$" over 32 chars had not returned after three minutes.
Compiling leniently on save lets an invalid pattern reach the database, which is the original bug: it was stored, then threw, and every later load threw on it too.
Strict compilation on load makes one bad stored pattern take down the entire rule set, leaving sensitivity scanning permanently unable to load.
PRIVACY. Drops the is_sensitive gate, so passwords and tokens get sent to the embedding model and cached as vectors.

why: App.OnSettingsChanged registers global hotkeys. RegisterHotKey binds WM_HOTKEY to the calling thread's message queue, so raising this from the pool kills every global hotkey silently until restart.
A deferred raise that reads the live field instead of the snapshot delivers the newest settings to every queued subscriber, so an earlier save is reported as the later one.
A view model that exposes ReactiveCommands but never calls ObserveCommandErrors leaves every failure in it silent. The IL-scan coverage test must catch that, or it is decoration.
If the reflection filter stops matching commands, ObserveCommandErrors silently subscribes to nothing and the coverage test passes vacuously for every view model.
Reporting must reach the installed sink; dropping to the Trace fallback while a sink exists leaves the user with no status message.
ReactiveObject also implements IHandleObservableErrors, so the looser filter matches every nested view-model property and double-reports their command failures.
Marking every dispatcher exception handled lets the app keep writing to the clip database after a failure that leaves managed state undefined.
Without a notification the user cannot tell a failed action from one that silently did nothing, which is the whole defect.
A fatal cause usually arrives wrapped in an AggregateException or a rethrow; only checking the outer type lets it through.
InsufficientMemoryException derives from OutOfMemoryException but is thrown before allocating, so it is recoverable; killing the app on it loses the user's session for nothing.
Without the rollback, any failure after the stash leaves the live path empty and the user's history under a .before-restore name that nothing looks for.
Stashing only the main file leaves stale -wal/-shm beside a different database, which SQLite may replay into it.
File.Move refuses an existing destination, so failing to clear the half-restored file makes the rollback a no-op.
The .before-restore copy is the user's only undo for a restore they did not mean to run; deleting the live files instead of renaming them destroys it.

Reverts the daily backup to a raw file copy. A checkpoint that cannot finish leaves committed frames in the WAL, and the copied .db then opens as 'database disk image is malformed' - an unopenable backup nobody notices until they need it.
Reverts the database path move to a raw file copy. The source is deleted immediately after the rename, so anything the copy missed is gone.
Writes the destination unencrypted. The copy would then be readable by anyone with the file, and unreadable by the app that expects the live key.
Leaves the connections in the pool, so the copied file is still held open and the caller's move or delete fails.
A truncated or differently-keyed leftover file at the destination cannot be opened, so failing to clear it first blocks every future copy to that path - backups stop happening and nothing says so.
find:
// and would block every future copy to this path, so clear it.
        File.Delete(destinationPath);
replace:
// and would block every future copy to this path, so clear it.
        _ = destinationPath;

why: Puts the column-dependent indexes back in the DDL batch that runs before the Ensure*Columns helpers. The batch then aborts with 'no such column' on any database predating those columns, so the app cannot open the user's history.

Skips the sort-order indexes entirely. They only work as a complete set - with partial coverage SQLite picks a pinned-prefixed index for an uncovered sort and fetches rows in an uncorrelated order, measured slower than no index at all.
byte_size was declared in CREATE TABLE but never added by a migration, so databases older than the column never gained it and could not be opened once an index referenced it.
The migration helpers are skipped when the stored version already matches, so new migration work is dead code unless the constant is bumped. Existing databases would silently never gain byte_size.
Puts index creation behind the schema-version gate, so an index dropped or lost on an up-to-date database is never restored - queries silently fall back to a scan.

Restores writing storage.json before flipping Current. A path move has already deleted the source by then, so a failed write leaves Current naming a path with no database - the workers restart there, create an empty one, and the real history is orphaned.

Flips Current before persisting even when nothing moved. A config-only write that fails then leaves the running session using settings that were never saved, silently diverging from what the next launch will read.

Restores joining whole-word tokens into one alternation. Ticking 'whole word' then silently turns a two-word AND search into an OR and returns clips containing either word, while the plain-text and FTS paths for the same query still require both.

Restores fusing the globally-ranked semantic top-K into every paged read. Load more is then handed the same semantic hits it already showed and appends them again, so a clip gets two view models whose selection and checkbox state diverge.

Restores paging on the on-screen row count. Semantic additions are not part of the query's offset space, so counting them advances the offset past query rows that were never shown - those clips match the search and appear on no page at all.

Stops clearing the semantic-addition mark when the query itself returns the clip on a later page. The offset then stays one row short for good, so every further Load more re-reads a row already on screen, discards it as a duplicate, and the list never grows again.

Restores trimming the fused page back to the page size. The lowest-ranked query rows are dropped to make room for semantic additions, and the next page resumes past them - so clips that matched the search are shown on no page.

Removes the call that syncs the embedding worker with the EnableSemanticSearch setting. Toggling semantic search then does nothing until the next launch: on leaves clips unembedded, off leaves the worker running.
Drops the disable branch, so turning semantic search off leaves the embedding worker running and consuming CPU and the SQLite write lock.

Runs each start/stop transition independently instead of chaining it onto the previous one. A rapid off->on toggle can then let the pending stop land after the start, leaving the worker off while semantic search is enabled.

Restores the unconditional restart in DatabaseMaintenanceScope.DisposeAsync. A worker the user had deliberately turned off (capture paused, semantic search disabled) comes back to life after any whole-database operation.

Makes ResetStalledOcrClaimsAsync a no-op. Clips stranded in the 'running' state by a stop are never returned to 'pending', and TryClaimForOcrAsync refuses to reclaim them - so they are never OCR'd again.
find: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET ocr_status = 'pending' WHERE ocr_status = 'running';";
replace: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET ocr_status = 'pending' WHERE ocr_status = 'no-such-status';";

why: Widens the reset to every clip regardless of status, so succeeded and failed clips are dragged back into the OCR backlog and the whole library is re-OCR'd on every restart.
find: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET ocr_status = 'pending' WHERE ocr_status = 'running';";

why: Removes the stalled-claim reset from EnqueueBacklogAsync. The backlog then re-queues nothing for clips a previous stop left mid-flight, so they stay invisible to OCR forever.

Drops the in-flight clear from StopAsync. Ids still queued when the reader stopped stay in the in-flight set, so Enqueue treats them as already queued and silently drops exactly the clips the stop interrupted.

Removes the start-of-loop sweep that returns stranded 'processing' rows to pending. A batch left behind by a stop or a crash is never re-selected by ClaimPendingEmbeddingsAsync, so those clips can never be embedded again while still counting as pending.

Clears the retry flag before the sweep instead of after it succeeds. A transient SQLite busy on the first attempt then strands those clips for the whole run - exactly the bug the sweep exists to prevent.

Drops the claim release from the model-missing path. The batch stays 'processing', which the claim query never re-selects, so the clips the comment promises to retry once the model is placed are stranded permanently.

Restores the fall-through into the bottom idle after a model-missing pass. The worker then waits two full idle periods before retrying, and the Poke that signals the model has been placed is swallowed by the wrong wait.
Makes ReleaseEmbeddingClaimsAsync release every processing row rather than only the named ones, so a batch another worker is actively embedding would be handed back out for duplicate work.
find: $"UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = 'pending' WHERE embedding_status = 'processing' AND id IN ({string.Join(",", paramNames)});";
replace: $"UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = 'pending' WHERE embedding_status = 'processing' AND (id IN ({string.Join(",", paramNames)}) OR 1=1);";

why: Widens the stalled sweep to reset successfully embedded clips too, which would silently re-embed the entire library on every worker start.
find: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = 'pending' WHERE embedding_status = 'processing';";
replace: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = 'pending' WHERE embedding_status IS NOT NULL;";

why: Drops the embedding purge from the sensitivity rebuild. A clip the user's new rules just classified as sensitive keeps the vector derived from its secret, and keeps counting as embedded.
find:
DELETE FROM clip_embeddings WHERE clip_id IN (SELECT id FROM clips WHERE is_sensitive = 1);
                UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = 'excluded' WHERE is_sensitive = 1;

why: Drops the un-exclude half of the rebuild. A clip that stopped being sensitive stays 'excluded', a state ClaimPendingEmbeddingsAsync never selects, so it can never be embedded again.
find: UPDATE clips SET embedding_status = NULL, embedding_attempts = 0 WHERE is_sensitive = 0 AND embedding_status = 'excluded';

why: Drops the semantic cache reload after a rule change. The cache still holds vectors for clips the user just made sensitive, so they stay semantically searchable for the rest of the session.
Drops the worker poke after a rule change, so clips that just became eligible wait a full idle period (or forever, if the worker is idle and never poked again) before being embedded.

Makes the rebuild blanket-clear is_sensitive instead of preserving hand-marked clips. Any sensitivity rule change silently declassifies every clip the user marked by hand, and the reconcile block below then hands those secrets to the embedding worker.
Stops SetSensitiveAsync recording that the verdict was the user's own. The clip is sensitive now, but the next rule change cannot tell it from a rule hit and declassifies it.
find: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET is_sensitive = $s, sensitivity_is_manual = $s WHERE id = $id;";
replace: command.CommandText = "UPDATE clips SET is_sensitive = $s WHERE id = $id;";

why: Adds the provenance column without recovering the marks that already exist. Every clip the user hand-marked before upgrading is declassified by the first rule change after it, which is exactly the data loss the column was added to stop.
Backfills every sensitive clip as manual, including rule-derived ones. Those verdicts freeze permanently: disabling or deleting the rule that produced them no longer declassifies the clip.
find:
WHERE is_sensitive = 1
                  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM clip_sensitivity_matches m WHERE m.clip_id = clips.id);

why: Reverts Alphabetical to SQLite's default BINARY collation, where every uppercase codepoint precedes every lowercase one. 'apple' sorts after 'Zebra' and any capitalised clip is banished to the front - not what a user means by alphabetical.
find: substr(c.content, 1, 64) COLLATE NOCASE ASC, c.content COLLATE NOCASE ASC
replace: substr(c.content, 1, 64) ASC, c.content COLLATE BINARY ASC

why: Drops COLLATE NOCASE from the index while the clause keeps it. An index is only usable by an ORDER BY that compares with the same collation, so the sort silently stops being served and falls back to sorting the whole library.
Reverts SortLines to the machine's culture, so the same clip sorts differently on different machines (on sv-SE 'A-ring' sorts after Z).
The over-correction: deterministic, but compares codepoints, so every capitalised line is banished ahead of every lowercase one ('Zebra' before 'apple') and accented letters land past 'z'.
Makes the identifier-producing camelCase transform locale-dependent again. Under tr-TR 'ID' lowercases to the dotless 'id', silently corrupting code on its way back to the clipboard.
Same for UpperCamelCase: under tr-TR 'identifier' becomes the dotted 'Identifier', which is not the identifier the user asked for.

The opposite over-correction, and the reason the split exists. Recasing prose is linguistic: forcing invariant turns Turkish 'istanbul' into 'ISTANBUL' instead of the correct dotted capital, which is the same corruption pointed the other way.
The leading character of every word after the first. Under tr-TR 'user id' becomes 'user' + dotted capital I, so the identifier is not the one the user asked for.
The tail of every word after the first. Under tr-TR 'user MAIL' becomes 'userMa' + dotless i + 'l'.

FromCamelCase capitalises the first character of its result. Under tr-TR 'identifierValue' gains a dotted capital I, so round-tripping an identifier through the two camel transforms no longer returns the original.
Drops the structural requirement, so a leading '|' alone is treated as table evidence again. A KQL, SQL or shell pipeline becomes a one-column HTML table and the original query is destroyed.
The over-correction: requires a border line even for box-drawing verticals, which no pipeline syntax uses. A borderless box table silently stops converting.
Stops the plain-text flavour decoding entities. The HTML flavour must escape prose around a converted table, so without this decode the user pastes a literal '&' into any plain-text target.
